541.quote_or_event: “Men frequently apply punishment wrongly: the innocent are put in prison, and the perpetrator of the crime is set at liberty.”
541.explanation: When Indra, disguised as a Brahmin, urges King Nami to punish thieves and robbers so that he may be a true Kshatriya, Nami answers that human punishment often lands on the wrong person.
541.tie_back: The Kural defines justice as investigating each case carefully and without favour before acting, and Nami's reply shows what goes wrong when that investigation is skipped: the innocent are jailed and the guilty go free.
541.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 9.30 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
541._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. The verse diagnoses the failure the Kural guards against, but Nami speaks as a renouncer who is doubtful about royal punishment altogether rather than as someone setting out a judicial procedure.

542.quote_or_event: When, through the fault of time, the power of the wish-fulfilling trees declined and the twins began to break the old laws, the people went to Rishabha, told him of the wrongdoing, and begged him to be their king, saying no one else like him could be found among them.
542.explanation: In Jain sacred history, kingship begins when nature's free provision fails. People who once lived from the wishing-trees now have to look to a ruler to keep order and sustain them.
542.tie_back: The Kural says that as all life looks to the sky for rain, subjects look to the king's sceptre. Hemacandra's account describes the moment the people of the first age turned from the failing wishing-trees to Rishabha's rule for their survival.
542.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book 1, ch. 2, part 8 ‘Coronation as king’ (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS; wisdomlib.org)
542._accuracy_note: Paraphrased from Johnson's translation as read on wisdomlib.org this session. The move from depending on nature to depending on a ruler parallels the Kural's rain image, but the Jain text uses wishing-trees, not rain, and attributes the decline to time rather than to the sky.

543.quote_or_event: “The example and advice of Samprati induced his vassals to embrace and patronize his creed, so that not only in his own kingdom, but also in the adjacent countries, the monks could practice their religion.”
543.explanation: Hemacandra's history of the Jain elders credits the Mauryan king Samprati with protection and patronage that let the mendicant order and its teaching flourish across and beyond his realm.
543.tie_back: The Kural says the just sceptre is what keeps the sages' scriptures and dharma standing, and the Samprati story makes the same claim from the Jain side: the monks could practise their dharma because a righteous king supported them.
543.source: Hemacandra, Pariśiṣṭaparvan (Sthavirāvalī) XI, as summarised by Hermann Jacobi; quoted in ‘The Jain Church After Mahavira’, jainworld.com
543._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against the jainworld.com page, which presents it as Jacobi's summary of Hemacandra, not a verse translation. It is a legendary, not historical, account. The Kural refers to the Vedas and Brahmin dharma, so the parallel is structural rather than doctrinal.

544.quote_or_event: “During his reign he taught, for the benefit of the people, the seventy-two sciences, of which writing is the first, arithmetic the most important, and the knowledge of omens the last, the sixty-four accomplishments of women, the hundred arts, and the three occupations of men.”
544.explanation: The Kalpa Sūtra presents Rishabha, called ‘First King’ before he became the first Tīrthaṅkara, as a ruler who spent his reign giving his people every skill they needed to live.
544.tie_back: The Kural pictures a king who embraces his people and is embraced in return by the whole world, and Rishabha, the Jain model of a king devoted to his subjects' welfare, is still revered by Jains at his feet.
544.source: Kalpa Sūtra, Life of Ṛṣabha §211 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884; sacred-texts.com)
544._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. It is a strong example of benevolent kingship, but the text does not state the Kural's reciprocal image of the world clinging to the king's feet.

545.quote_or_event: “In the night in which the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra was brought into the family of the Gñâtris their silver increased, their gold increased; their riches, corn, majesty, and kingdom increased; their army, train, treasure, storehouse, town, seraglio, subjects, and glory increased”
545.explanation: Because the realm prospered from the moment the future Tīrthaṅkara was conceived, his parents named him Vardhamāna, ‘the Increaser’.
545.tie_back: The Kural links righteous rule to abundant harvests in the land, and the Kalpa Sūtra likewise tells of a royal house whose corn, treasure and subjects multiplied in the presence of great merit.
545.source: Kalpa Sūtra, Life of Mahāvīra §90 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884; sacred-texts.com)
545._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com (quoted up to a semicolon in mid-sentence). The prosperity comes from the merit of the Jina-to-be, not from just government, and the text does not mention rain, so this is a partial next-best match.

546.quote_or_event: When Bharata, the first Cakravartin, and his brother Bāhubali faced each other with their armies, they agreed to settle their dispute through personal contests, beginning with an unblinking eye-fight, instead of a battle that would slaughter their soldiers. Bāhubali won, but at the moment of victory he renounced his kingdom and became a monk.
546.explanation: The best-known Jain story about royal conflict refuses to let the spear decide. Armies are set aside, and the real victory turns out to be Bāhubali's conquest of his own pride and anger.
546.tie_back: The Kural says a king's victory comes from his sceptre, not his spear. The Bharata–Bāhubali story likewise declines to let weapons and soldiers settle a royal quarrel.
546.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book 1, ch. 5, part 11 ‘The fight between Bharata and Bāhubali’ (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS; wisdomlib.org)
546._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. The chapter's contents were confirmed this session only through a search excerpt of the wisdomlib text. The story rejects the spear as the Kural does, but it puts restraint and renunciation in the sceptre's place, not just rule.

547.quote_or_event: “Whenever you die, O king, and leave all pleasant things behind, the Law alone, and nothing else in this world, will save you, O monarch.”
547.explanation: Queen Kamalāvatī warns King Ishukāra, who is about to seize property, that neither wealth nor power can protect a ruler; only dharma can.
547.tie_back: The Kural says the king guards the world and justice in turn guards the king. The queen tells her king the same thing: the Law alone protects him.
547.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 14.40 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
547._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. The idea that dharma protects the ruler matches closely, but the Jain verse means protection beyond death, while the Kural means the security of a king's reign.

548.quote_or_event: “A cut-throat enemy will not do him such harm as his own perversity will do him; the man without pity will feel repentance in the hour of death.”
548.explanation: The sage tells King Śreṇika that a person's own wrong conduct does more damage than any outside foe, and in the same sermon he says the self is ‘friend and foe’ (20.37).
548.tie_back: The Kural's king, inaccessible and failing to do justice, is brought down by his own conduct ‘even without an enemy’, which is exactly the Jain claim that one's own perversity outdoes any enemy.
548.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 20.48 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
548._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. The self-ruin theme fits well, but in context the verse is about a lapsed monk, not a ruler who neglects his subjects.

549.quote_or_event: “A king will be the punisher of those transgressing boundaries. Seated on a very high throne, consecrated first, having at hand the fourfold army, he should have unbroken commands.”
549.explanation: When the earlier laws of reproach fail and people start doing wrong, Rishabha explains that a consecrated king is needed to punish transgressors, and he is then made the first king.
549.tie_back: The Kural says that protecting the people and curbing crime by punishment is a king's proper work, not a blemish. In Jain sacred history the office of king was created for exactly that purpose.
549.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book 1, ch. 2, part 8 ‘Coronation as king’ (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS; wisdomlib.org)
549._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Johnson's translation on wisdomlib.org. It matches the Kural's view that punishment belongs properly to kingship, though it does not cover the Kural's points about protection from outside enemies or from the king's own exactions.

550.quote_or_event: “Virodhi Himsa is the kind of injury which is necessarily committed in defense of person and property, against thieves, robbers, dacoits, assailants and enemies, in meeting their aggression, and in causing the least possible injury, necessary in the circumstances, in which one may find oneself.”
550.explanation: Jain ethics allows a householder only defensive injury against aggressors, and only the least injury the situation requires. Monks must avoid even that.
550.tie_back: The Kural approves of a king executing murderers the way a farmer pulls weeds. Jainism will accept force against violent offenders only as minimal, defensive injury and would not call execution a good.
550.source: ‘The Concept of Himsa’, jainworld.com (text from V.A. Sangave's Jaina Path of Ahimsa; page also credited to Acharya Mahapragya)
550._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against the jainworld.com page; the page's authorship credit is ambiguous. Jain ahimsa is in real tension with this kural's endorsement of the death penalty, so this is an honest next-best match, not an endorsement.
